name: Elimination diet
summary: Temporarily removing suspected trigger foods, then reintroducing them one at a time; established for diagnosing food allergy and eosinophilic esophagitis, with little trial evidence for finding skin triggers.
lead: An elimination diet, also called an exclusion or oligoantigenic diet, is a diagnostic procedure for identifying foods that cause adverse effects, whether from food allergy, food intolerance or other causes. A suspected food is removed for about two weeks to two months while symptoms are monitored, and foods are then reintroduced one at a time .
claims: Removing trigger foods can reveal and clear personal acne or skin triggers
Elimination diets identify food allergies and intolerances

name: Low-histamine diet
summary: An elimination diet cutting aged, fermented and stored foods to curb flushing and skin symptoms blamed on histamine; the concept and the evidence are both thin.
lead: A low-histamine diet is an eating pattern that restricts foods high in histamine, or thought to promote its release or block its breakdown, with the aim of reducing symptoms attributed to histamine intolerance. Reported symptoms include flushing, itching, headaches and digestive complaints . Typical advice is to eat fresh food, avoid stored leftovers, and limit fermented foods, aged cheese, cured meats and alcohol .
claims: Cutting high-histamine foods reduces facial flushing and skin redness.
Low DAO enzyme activity explains reactions to food.
A low-histamine diet helps eczema.

name: Paleo diet
summary: A whole-food, no-grain, no-dairy diet built on a contested picture of ancestral eating; short trials show some metabolic effects, long-term evidence is thin.
lead: The Paleolithic or paleo diet is an eating pattern based on foods its proponents believe pre-agricultural humans ate. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, nuts, roots and meat, and excludes dairy, grains, legumes, refined sugar, processed oils and often salt and alcohol .
claims: Humans are genetically adapted to a pre-agricultural diet, so grains and dairy cause modern disease.
Paleo eating improves leanness and body composition.
The diet treats autoimmune and inflammatory disease.

name: Whole30
summary: A 30-day strict elimination diet of sugar, grains, dairy, alcohol and legumes; popular as a reset, with no controlled trials of its own.
lead: Whole30 is a 30-day elimination diet created in 2009 by Melissa Hartwig (now Melissa Urban) and Dallas Hartwig. Participants remove added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and (in the original version) legumes and soy for a month, then reintroduce foods one at a time to observe effects .
claims: Thirty days off sugar, grains, dairy and alcohol resets energy, sleep and cravings.
The reintroduction phase identifies personal food sensitivities.
Excluding legumes and whole grains is necessary.

name: Bryan Johnson Blueprint diet
summary: The mostly vegan, early-eating plan of longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson; widely shared, tested only on himself.
lead: The Blueprint diet is the largely vegan eating plan that American entrepreneur Bryan Johnson follows as part of Blueprint, his longevity protocol announced in October 2021 as Project Blueprint and later a company sold under the slogan "Don't Die" . Johnson says his goal is to lower the biological age of his organs, and he publishes his meals, supplements and biomarker results .
claims: The Blueprint diet reverses biological aging.
Eating early and finishing by late morning supports longevity.

name: Longevity / Blue Zones diets
summary: Plant-leaning diets modelled on regions reported for long-lived residents; popular, but the underlying longevity data are disputed.
lead: Blue Zones diets are eating patterns modelled on regions reported to have unusually many long-lived people: Sardinia, Okinawa, Nicoya in Costa Rica, Icaria in Greece, and later Martinique . They are generally described as predominantly plant-based, alongside physical activity, low stress and social ties .
claims: Eating like Blue Zone residents extends lifespan.
The diets keep skin and appearance youthful.

name: Orange juice / vitamin C diet
summary: Heavy orange juice or vitamin C intake for skin, resting on vitamin C's collagen role; untested for appearance and sugar-heavy.
lead: The orange juice or vitamin C diet refers to consuming large amounts of citrus juice or vitamin C, in the belief that it improves skin. Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis, and this role is the basis for the appearance claims .
claims: Mega-dose vitamin C or orange juice improves skin quality.

name: Cinnamon / apple cider vinegar shots
summary: Diluted apple cider vinegar (sometimes with cinnamon) taken for fat loss and skin; no high-quality trials back the appearance claims.
lead: Cinnamon and apple cider vinegar (ACV) shots are a home-made drink in which diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes with cinnamon, is swallowed in the belief that it helps with fat loss, bloating or skin. Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice first to alcohol and then to acetic acid, and is about 5% acetic acid and 94% water.

name: Fat burner supplements
summary: Stimulant-heavy supplement blends sold for fat loss; no category-level efficacy data and a documented record of liver injury and adulteration reports.
lead: Fat burner supplements are over-the-counter products, usually multi-ingredient stimulant blends, marketed to increase metabolic rate or reduce body fat. They fall within the broader category of weight-loss dietary supplements, which in the United States are regulated under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA): no pre-market approval is required and the FDA generally acts only after a product is on sale.

name: Green tea / EGCG
summary: Green tea catechin sold as a mild fat-burner; mostly lab and animal evidence, with liver-safety warnings for concentrated extracts.
lead: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is the most abundant catechin in tea, a polyphenol formed from epigallocatechin and gallic acid. Dried green tea leaves contain about 7,380 mg per 100 g, far more than black tea, in which most catechins are converted during processing. Green tea and concentrated green tea extracts are sold as mild 'thermogenic' or fat-loss supplements.

name: Vitamin A (retinyl palmitate) from liver
summary: Preformed vitamin A from liver is a real nutrient with a documented toxicity threshold; no appearance trials exist.
lead: Preformed vitamin A, which includes retinol and retinyl esters such as retinyl palmitate, occurs in animal liver and in some supplements. Some diet communities eat liver or take liver-derived products for skin, vision and general nutrition. Hypervitaminosis A is the toxicity caused by excess preformed vitamin A, and Wikipedia lists liver, supplements and prescription medicines as the usual sources.

name: Cod liver oil
summary: A traditional vitamin A, D and omega-3 oil with a long medical history; no appearance trials, and its vitamin A content is the main safety issue.
lead: Cod liver oil is a dietary supplement made from the liver of Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua). Like other fish oils it contains the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA, and unlike most it also contains substantial vitamins A and D. One tablespoon (13.6 g) provides about 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A and 34 micrograms (1,360 IU) of vitamin D according to USDA figures cited by Wikipedia.

name: Fermented cod liver oil / butter oil (Weston A. Price)
summary: A Weston A. Price Foundation supplement pairing of fermented cod liver oil and butter oil; no clinical studies found.
lead: Fermented cod liver oil combined with high-vitamin butter oil is a supplement pairing associated with the Weston A. Price Foundation, a nutrition advocacy group co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig to promote the research of Canadian dentist Weston A. Price (1870 to 1948). Followers use it as a source of fat-soluble vitamins, aiming for dental, skeletal and facial-structure benefits.
claims: Traditional diets rich in animal fats protect teeth and facial structure.

name: Weston A. Price diet
summary: Traditional-foods philosophy from a 1930s dentist's travels; influential in diet circles, with no trials of the diet itself.
lead: The Weston A. Price diet is a "traditional foods" dietary philosophy derived from the work of Weston A. Price (1870-1948), a Canadian-born American dentist who compared the diets, teeth and facial development of traditional and Westernised populations in his 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration. Proponents draw on it to argue that refined flour, sugar and industrial vegetable fats lead to dental decay and narrower facial structure, themes that overlap with appearance-focused communities.

name: Ray Peat diet
summary: Dairy, fruit, juice and low-PUFA eating from Raymond Peat's writings; popular for hormone claims, with no trials.
lead: The Ray Peat diet is an eating pattern inspired by the writings of Raymond Peat, an American author on nutrition and physiology. Followers describe it as "pro-metabolic" and aimed at correcting hormonal imbalances and raising metabolic rate. Typical elements are milk, cheese, fruit and fruit juice, root vegetables, eggs, shellfish, muscle and organ meats, collagen, and saturated fats such as butter and coconut oil, while polyunsaturated fats are avoided.
claims: The diet raises metabolism and corrects hormonal imbalance
Peat grew about an inch in his 40s using DHEA

name: Low-PUFA diet
summary: Cutting seed oils, nuts and fatty fish on oxidation grounds; popular in Ray Peat circles, untested as a looks strategy.
lead: A low-PUFA diet is an eating pattern that minimises polyunsaturated fatty acids, found in vegetable seed oils, nuts, seeds and fatty fish. In online metabolism and appearance circles it is most associated with the Ray Peat diet, whose followers say PUFAs are unstable, oxidise easily and burden metabolism.
claims: PUFAs oxidise and become toxic in the body, so should be minimised

name: Anti-estrogen diet (cruciferous / DIM)
summary: Eating broccoli or taking DIM to cut estrogen: popular in T-optimization circles, but no trial in men shows it changes anything visible.
lead: The anti-estrogen diet is a lifestyle practice in which people eat cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage, kale and Brussels sprouts, or take supplements of diindolylmethane (DIM), with the stated aim of lowering estrogen activity or shifting estrogen metabolism, usually in order to raise the ratio of testosterone to estrogen. DIM is a compound formed in the body from indole-3-carbinol, which comes from these vegetables, and it is sold as a dietary supplement.

name: Testosterone-boosting diet (eggs, oysters, red meat)
summary: Eggs, oysters and beef as a T booster: nutrient deficiencies matter, but no trial shows the diet lifts testosterone in men who are already replete.
lead: The testosterone-boosting diet is a food-based approach in which people emphasise eggs, oysters, red meat and similar foods, marketed or believed to raise testosterone. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a way to support muscularity, masculine features and energy.

name: Oysters / shellfish for zinc
summary: Oysters are the richest food source of zinc, used as a T-support food; benefit is tied to correcting deficiency.
lead: Oysters and other shellfish are eaten in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a concentrated food source of zinc, a mineral linked to testosterone production. Wikipedia describes oysters as having the most zinc of any food, with two oysters (28 g) supplying the US reference daily intake.

name: Boron + zinc + D3 test-boost stack
summary: Boron, zinc and D3 together as a testosterone stack: each has a plausible hormone link, but the combo has no trial behind it.
lead: The boron, zinc and vitamin D3 stack is a combination of over-the-counter supplements taken in the belief that together they raise testosterone. Each ingredient has some published link to hormone physiology, and the combination is discussed in supplement and looksmaxxing communities.

name: Soy avoidance
summary: Avoiding soy to protect testosterone: meta-analyses find no effect of soy or isoflavones on male hormones.
lead: Soy avoidance is the practice of cutting soy foods from the diet because of fears that their isoflavones, plant compounds classed as phytoestrogens, lower testosterone, raise estrogen or feminise men. The idea circulates widely in fitness and looksmaxxing communities.

name: Plastic / endocrine disruptor avoidance
summary: Dodging BPA and phthalates to protect testosterone: regulators are tightening limits, but avoidance trials in men are absent.
lead: Plastic and endocrine disruptor avoidance is a lifestyle practice of limiting exposure to BPA, phthalates and similar plastic additives in order to protect testosterone and hormone balance. People swap plastic containers for glass or steel and avoid certain packaged foods and receipts.

name: Tap water / fluoride avoidance
summary: Swapping tap for filtered or spring water to dodge fluoride; health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no appearance data exist.
lead: Tap water / fluoride avoidance is a lifestyle practice in which people drink and sometimes wash with filtered, bottled or spring water instead of municipal tap water, mainly to avoid fluoride, and sometimes chlorine. In appearance-focused communities it is presented as part of a health-and-skin routine.

name: Filtered / spring water
summary: Drinking filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine; tap water is heavily regulated and no appearance benefit is documented.
lead: Filtered or spring water is drinking water treated with a home filter or bought bottled from a spring, used by some people in place of tap water to avoid fluoride and chlorine.

name: Alcohol avoidance (sober maxxing)
summary: Quitting alcohol for clearer skin; alcohol carries well-documented health risks, but appearance gains are untested.
lead: Alcohol avoidance, sometimes called sober maxxing, is the practice of quitting or abstaining from alcohol, in appearance communities often for the stated aim of improving skin.

name: Quitting smoking / vaping
summary: Quitting smoking or vaping to slow skin aging; smoker's face is documented, quitting's facial reversal is thinly studied.
lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is a practice appearance communities cite for reducing premature skin aging. Smoker's face describes facial changes seen in smokers, including a characteristic wrinkle pattern and sallow grey skin tone.

name: Caffeine avoidance
summary: Dropping caffeine to reduce puffiness and improve sleep; sleep effects are documented, puffiness is untested.
lead: Caffeine avoidance is cutting out coffee, tea and energy drinks, in appearance communities often for the stated aim of reducing facial puffiness and improving sleep.

name: Coffee for skin / Cold brew
summary: Coffee and cold brew pitched for skin; general health data exist but skin claims are untested here.
lead: Coffee for skin / cold brew refers to claims in appearance communities about coffee, including cold brew, and skin or looks, whether by drinking or topical use.

name: Nutritional yeast / B-vitamin loading
summary: Eating fortified yeast flakes or stacking B-complex for skin and hair; the vitamins are real, the cosmetic payoff is unstudied.
lead: Nutritional yeast, informally called "nooch", is a deactivated yeast, usually a strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sold as yellow flakes or powder and used in vegan cooking as a cheese-like seasoning . In looksmaxxing and wider wellness circles, "B-vitamin loading" refers to eating nutritional yeast or taking B-complex supplements in generous amounts in the hope of improving skin, hair and nails.

name: Heavy cream / butter diet
summary: A very high-fat dairy take on low-carb eating; nobody has trialled it for looks, and butter raises LDL.
lead: The heavy cream / butter diet is a high-fat dairy variant of low-carbohydrate eating, in which large amounts of butter and cream supply a major share of calories. It is discussed in appearance communities mainly as a way to lose fat or to keep meals simple while eating very low carbohydrate.
